name: The State as natural and prior to the individual
plain_explanation: Aristotle argues that families combine into villages, villages into a self-sufficient State, and that although the State comes later in time, it is 'prior by nature' to the family and the individual, since a person (like a hand cut off from a body) cannot truly fulfil their purpose except as part of a State.
precise_definition: Aristotle's organic conception of political community, in which the State, though the last stage in a natural sequence of family and village, is metaphysically prior to its parts because 'what each thing is when fully developed we call its nature,' and a part (like a severed hand) can be defined only by the function it performs within the functioning whole.
why_it_mattered: It grounds Aristotle's claim that 'the end of the State is the good life,' not mere economic exchange or crime prevention, and that 'he who founded the State was the greatest of benefactors,' since law and full human fulfilment depend on it.
historical_origin: Original to Aristotle's Politics, drawing on his biological conception of 'nature' as an organism's mature, functional end-state.
examples: 'A hand, when the body is destroyed, is... no longer a hand' -- illustrating that a part is defined by its function within a living whole.
'The State is the union of families and villages in a perfect and self-sufficing life... a happy and honourable life.'
influence_on_later_thinkers: The organic analogy for the State recurs throughout later political theory, both liberal and totalitarian.
